destructiveRule: destructive counts NEW retirements only: destructive = sum(newRetirements), destructiveShare = destructive / population (the whole served tier-1 population, not the keyspace). The rule is stated at the top of the gate module as DESTRUCTIVE_RULE, and the UNACCOUNTED refusal now tests unaccountedDestructive (new retirements on a basis the roll cannot hold) -- without which a county whose already-retired keyspace has no index of its own keys could never publish again, which is exactly the state Williamson is in today.

LESSON: A set-difference gate is only as right as its READER, and a reader that is right can still be the wrong number if a second writer in the same path uses a different reader. On this store the retirement marks themselves carry the authority string of the comparison that wrote them -- grouping retired rows by that string is a cheap, decisive way to find out WHO emptied a population, and it should be the first query in any incident of this shape. It is how this lane found the second writer after two prior lanes had reasoned about the first.

When a test fake answers an existence probe (`to_regclass`) for one table, a new reader in the code under test will silently get a refusal instead of the error the test is about -- and the failure lands in tests that look unrelated. Adding a reader means auditing every fake that answers existence probes.

Reading only the part of a failing test log that matches the row ids you expect is how a red branch ships. Read the whole failing set, or CI will read it for you. This lane's own logs had 19 publish failures and I reported 5 -- the filter, not the log, is what hid them.
DEAD-END: Trying to close the Williamson hazard from inside the factory with a pre-bake refusal: the writer that emptied it runs after promotion, inside the bake subprocess. Do not spend another lane on a smarter pre-bake comparison for that pass; the fix has to be at the pass or in the bake's contract.
